scenario: AITA for not wanting to cover my co-workers shift so he can attend his sister's memorial? | My co-worker asked if I can cover his 2pm-10pm (most likely schedule but could be 3-10pm) shift so he could attend his sister's memorial. I don't know the details and wether or not he asked me the day of her death. The place we work, schedules us 1 week in advanced every Tuesday so he has known his schedule for at least a week prior to the day he asked me. Our work offers us the option to work part of our shift and have someone come in and cover the rest of their shift if there is someone available to do so via our employee attendance system online. For the schedule my co-worker is on that day he would have an answer by 4pm whether it be a yes or no for someone to cover him. My thinking is that he put in for a partial shift request but no one was available so he started texting people to ask if they can come in. Me being one of them. My co-worker texted me asking if I can come in so he can attend his sister's memorial at 7:30pm (paraphrasing but pretty much the gist of the message) I absolutely hate this job so I said I'm not able to come in even though I'm free to. My co-worker has asked me to come in for him a couple of times before and I came in for him on one occasion. I asked him to cover one of my shifts later on so the way I see it we're even on owing favors. He messages me right after I decline with "Of course not" (his exact words) Made me feel like an asshole so here I am. Am I the asshole?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether you’re "the asshole" depends on perspective—but **I’d lean toward 1 (not the asshole)** with some important context. Here’s why: ### **Why You’re Not the Asshole (1):** 1. **You’re Not Obligated to Cover Shifts for Free** - Your workplace *offers* partial-shift coverage as an option, but it’s not mandatory. If no one was available through the system, your co-worker had to ask people individually. You’re under no obligation to say yes, especially if you’re unhappy at work. - **Favor balance?** If he’s asked you before and you’ve helped once, that’s fair—but it doesn’t mean you owe him another one. Life isn’t a ledger of favors. 2. **You Have No Insight into the Situation** - You don’t know if this is a last-minute emergency, a deeply personal loss, or just a personal preference. His response ("Of course not") suggests he didn’t expect you to drop everything for him, which implies he wasn’t asking out of entitlement. - His phrasing ("so he can attend his sister’s memorial") was likely a way to explain why he needed coverage—not a demand. 3. **Your Emotional State Matters** - You said you *hate* this job. That’s valid. If you’re already resentful, forcing yourself to cover shifts for others—especially when the system already failed to provide coverage—could make things worse for you. - **Burnout is real.** If you’re already stretched thin, saying no isn’t selfish—it’s self-preservation. 4. **His Reaction Wasn’t Angry—It Was Resigned** - His "Of course not" wasn’t a scolding; it was a sigh of disappointment. He likely expected you to say no anyway. That doesn’t make you the bad guy—it just means he’s used to people declining. --- ### **Where the Gray Area Lies (But Still Not "Asshole" Level):** - **Could you have been more empathetic?** Maybe. A simple *"I’m not in a good headspace for this, but I’m sorry about your loss"* would’ve softened the blow. But his reaction suggests he didn’t hold it against you. - **Did you handle it poorly?** Yes, but not in a way that makes you a jerk. You were direct, and his response wasn’t hostile—just resigned. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not the Asshole)** You weren’t wrong for saying no. His reaction shows he didn’t expect you to, and your own happiness (or lack thereof) at work is valid. That said, **next time**, you could acknowledge the situation without committing: > *"I’m not available, but I’m sorry about your sister. Wishing you strength."* This keeps it kind while still standing your ground. But honestly? You did nothing wrong here.
